claims.statement: The OpenWiki bundle is generated through the `wiki-update` Nx target on the infrastructure-as-code project, whose command is `node scripts/wiki-generate.mjs`; the launcher resolves the provider, maps only the selected provider's credential at the point of use, and spawns `openwiki code --update --print`, while `wiki-plan`, `wiki-maintain`, `okf-lint` and `okf-governance` are the four sibling targets around it.

`scripts/wiki-generate.mjs` refuses to start unless `OPENWIKI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is set to an integer of at least 16384, so a direct invocation cannot bypass the cap; a truncated turn closes the model loop's stop condition and produces a silent exit-0 zero-page run.

A run message must be passed in the `WIKI_RUN_MESSAGE` environment variable, never through `nx --args`: Nx appends args to a shell command line unquoted, so the message arrives split into many words and the paid run goes unscoped. The launcher passes it as a single argv element with no shell.

The wiki-maintain workflow is merge-triggered on pushes to `main` with a quiet-period debounce implemented as `concurrency` plus `cancel-in-progress` plus an initial sleep, and it is deliberately never a required branch-protection context because it is a paid and occasionally slow job.

There is no scheduled maintenance job: on a feature branch the wiki is refreshed through the feature-completion checklist, and on `main` only by the merge-triggered workflow — neither has a `schedule:` trigger.

`scripts/wiki-maintain.mjs` never consults the generator's exit status: it judges a slice by the pages that landed in the working tree, by bundle conformance and by whether the regeneration policy permitted every written path, because feature 043 measured 12 minutes of paid work writing one `index.md` and exiting 0.

Maintenance exit codes distinguish three non-broken outcomes from two failures: `0` means a plan was produced, every attempted slice verified, or nothing to do — including `--execute` stopping before any paid generation because the checkout's run record is behind `main`'s; `1` means a slice failed verification; `2` means bad usage, an unreadable run record, a missing credential or a failed preflight; and `3` means the run stopped at its page or wall-clock budget with work carried forward in the committed backlog and is explicitly not a failure, on the same reasoning that separates runner starvation from a red build. The workflow maps `0` and `3` to the two non-broken outcomes and `1`/`2` to `failed`, so the run's exit code is never confused with the generator's.

The run record `openwiki/.maintenance-state.json` is committed because CI runners are ephemeral and the marker must advance even on a run that produced no proposal; it is distinct from the tool's own `openwiki/.last-update.json`, which advances only when wiki content changed. The step that commits it pushes with a `[skip ci]` message and the job's own skip check recognises both that message and a bundle-only change, so the workflow cannot trigger itself; a push race with `main` is handled by rebuilding the commit on the current tip and merging the record three ways, never by replaying this run's record over a newer one.

Neither the page budget nor the wall-clock budget is a monetary bound: OpenWiki emits no token or cost figure of its own, so the wall-clock budget exists only to bound occupancy of the single shared CI runner.

The OKF conformance gate (`scripts/check-openwiki-okf.mjs`) is offline, keyless and fail-closed with no skip flag, resolving repository-relative `resource` links against the working tree while only shape-checking external ones, so it cannot fail because a third-party host is down; drift rule V12 is the sole rule that warns without affecting the exit code.

Rule V16 holds a page that openwiki has covered (an entry in `openwiki/.page-manifest.json`) to the sha256 its verified Claims sidecar certifies, with the invariant defined once in `scripts/openwiki-claims.mjs`; a hand edit of such a page makes openwiki refuse every later run until the page is uncovered.
The conformance gate is fail-closed on an absent, empty or partially-written bundle with deliberately no skip flag, mirroring the fail-closed posture other repository gates use.

The `mermaid` and `jsdom` packages are optional peer dependencies of the generator whose absence is silent: without the real parser a diagram that fails only the strict check is rewritten in place into a plain `text` fence, with a comment naming the parser error, while the run still exits 0 and every gate still passes — so guard tests assert that the toolchain image and CI's locked install ship the same parser set (both exact pins beside `openwiki` in `tools/openwiki-generator/package.json`).

The managed `<!-- OPENWIKI:START -->…<!-- OPENWIKI:END -->` block in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` must already be byte-identical to what the pinned generator writes, because openwiki rewrites that block on every run while the regeneration policy permits only an agent to write `AGENTS.md`; a mismatch would fail every slice and hold the marker indefinitely.

The generation brief, the regeneration policy and the protection manifest are all declared never-written, because a process must not be able to rewrite the file that constrains it; the brief is the sole remediation surface when a gate rejects generated content, since the gates have no allowlist.

The canonical-home rule routes a durable learning by the concept's front matter: a concept carrying a resolving `resource` is a derived summary so the learning goes into the cited source, while a concept with no `resource` is authoritative and listed under `authoritative:` in the protection manifest so the learning goes into the concept. The governance gate enforces the classification in both directions: G11 rejects a concept that is neither a resolving derived summary nor a listed authoritative one (and one that is both), and G12 rejects an authoritative concept whose effective policy is `regenerate`, because a summary of nothing could only be paraphrased.

The governance gate (`scripts/check-openwiki-governance.mjs`) is offline, keyless and fail-closed with no skip flag, and checks that every documentation path carries a declared regeneration policy, that `actor: generator` appears only inside the bundle, that every event-driven entry names its events, that protected passages still match their fingerprints (a removed passage failing as a removal), and that `CLAUDE.md` holds only its index and machine-managed regions.
Both gates run as steps of the same always-on `okf` CI job, each preceded by its own `--selftest` so that a rule which silently stopped detecting its case would turn the build red.

CI and the dev container must run the same pinned generator version (`openwiki@0.7.1`): the workflow cannot resolve it as a workspace dependency and instead installs it from a committed lockfile in `tools/openwiki-generator/`, while the dev container bakes a global install at image-build time, and a guard test reads the `npm install -g openwiki@<v>` command line from the Dockerfile and fails if it names a version other than the one in the locked manifest — otherwise the two environments would silently disagree about the output the gates judge.

The wiki-maintain job installs the generator from `tools/openwiki-generator/`, a standalone pnpm workspace holding exact pins for `openwiki`, `mermaid` and `jsdom` plus its own `pnpm-lock.yaml`, via `pnpm --dir tools/openwiki-generator install --frozen-lockfile`, and puts that directory's `node_modules/.bin` first on `PATH`; the verify step fails unless `command -v openwiki` resolves there, and a guard test rejects any run-time resolution (global install, `npx`, `pnpm add`) because the previous `npm install -g openwiki@0.7.1` pinned only `openwiki` and resolved its whole transitive tree at run time.

`tools/openwiki-generator` is deliberately its own pnpm workspace root outside the root workspace's `frontend/*` and `packages/*` globs, so the root's settings (which set no cooldown) do not apply, and it sets `minimumReleaseAge: 4320` (three days, Renovate's catch-all); pnpm enforces that window both at resolve time (a lockfile regeneration cannot pick a younger transitive) and at install time (a frozen install fails `ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION`). Its `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` is reserved for security-floor exceptions — each entry must be one exact `name@x.y.z` required by an `overrides:` floor in the same file — and guard tests fail a cooldown under three days, a name-only or ranged exclusion or one with no matching floor, a range instead of an exact pin, a lockfile that disagrees with the manifest, or a root glob that swallows the directory.

The wiki-maintain job runs the installed-generator guard tests after the locked install and before any paid work, and fails the step if any check SKIPPED — a skip reads as a pass, and the checks that describe the pinned generator skip in every job where it is not installed.

Drift is not an input to `planSlices` itself — that function takes only the paths changed since the run-record marker plus the carried-forward backlog — but `computePlan` adds up to `DRIFT_PAGES_PER_RUN` (2) drifted concepts on top, taken oldest-stamp-first from the page budget left over after change-driven and backlog work, so a concept whose source moved before the marker is re-planned without a hand-seeded sweep. Drift beyond the bound is reported and never written to the backlog; a directory `resource` is unplannable because any commit under it re-flags the page; a parked page is excluded and listed; and a drift candidate the open proposal already holds fresh is skipped as `on the open proposal` — only drift, because freshness compares commit dates and a merged branch keeps its earlier date.

The drift comparison has one definition in `scripts/openwiki-drift.mjs`, imported by V12, by wiki-maintain's stale-page verifier and by its drift planner so the three cannot disagree; it compares the cited source's last **commit** date (never mtime, because a fresh checkout restamps every file, with V12 falling back to mtime only for an untracked source) against the newest of `generated.at`, `verified.at` and `timestamp`, and reports a source that cannot be judged or a page with no usable stamp rather than guessing.

The target's `OPENWIKI_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=16384` is a floor, not the effective cap: the `fireworks` provider row sets `maxOutputTokens: 65536` and the launcher raises the cap to it without ever lowering an explicit higher value, because DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reasons inside its output budget and a worker writing a whole page in one `write_file` turn exhausted 16384 tokens before its tool call; the `anthropic` row sets no raise because the Anthropic SDK refuses a non-streaming request whose `max_tokens` implies more than ten minutes.

The wiki-maintain workflow runs from the current tip of `main` rather than the event commit (while the self-skip decision still reads the event commit), so a queued overlapping run plans from the record an earlier run committed instead of repaying work that cannot be published.

The conformance gate's rule table in `specs/043-openwiki-okf/data-model.md` stops at V15; rule V16 (a covered page's bytes must still hash to the `pageVersion` its verified Claims sidecar certifies) exists only in code, defined once in `scripts/openwiki-claims.mjs` and shared with `wiki-maintain`'s post-generation link rewrite, so a reader looking for V16 in the data model will not find it.

The always-on `okf` guardrails job installs the workspace (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`) before running either gate because both gates import the root `yaml` dependency, without which each dies on `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before checking anything — and it deliberately does NOT run the gates' own unit tests, because the `naming` job's shell-expanded `node --test scripts/__tests__/*.test.mjs` glob already picks them up, so a broken gate test reddens `naming` rather than `okf`.

Because branch protection requires the `guardrails*` context glob, any job placed in `guardrails.yml` is a required merge context by construction — which is why the governance gate was added as steps inside the existing `okf` job (a new job would owe its own failure-digest step for no benefit), while the paid `wiki-maintain` workflow is deliberately never a required context and must not be added to branch protection, so the two gates block a merge but a stale bundle never does.

The maintenance trigger's debounce is bounded by a six-hour maximum deferral: `shouldDeferMaintenance` runs immediately once the oldest commit the run record has not covered reaches `MAX_DEFERRAL_SECONDS` (21600 s, at-or-past rather than strictly greater so a stream pinned at the ceiling cannot defer forever), and that age is derived from git commit dates rather than from a timer because the debounce works by cancelling the waiting run — any timer it held would die with it, while git state survives. A `workflow_dispatch` run bypasses the wait entirely.

`node scripts/wiki-maintain.mjs --claims-audit` is a second offline, keyless, model-free check beside `wiki-plan`: it loads openwiki's own `RepositoryEvidenceResolver` from the install the `openwiki` binary on `PATH` resolves to, re-resolves the `repo://` evidence of every Claims sidecar whose page exists, and lists the pages openwiki will force into the next run as a mandatory full paid regeneration whatever was requested (exiting 2 when no such install is on `PATH`).

A forced page is labelled *churn citations only: avoidable* when every one of its issues is a churn citation — a lockfile basename, a `.env.deploy` digest pin, a line-addressed `allowlist.yaml` entry, or a cited range containing an `@sha256:` digest — and the generation brief's Claims-evidence rule forbids citing those precisely because such a citation goes stale on routine commits that change no fact the page states, forcing the page to be paid for again.

The planner caps a slice at `MAX_PAGES_PER_SLICE` (8) pages when refreshing concepts that already exist and at `MAX_NEW_PAGES_PER_SLICE` (3) when creating new ones, one bundle area per slice, and never mixes the two kinds in one slice — the lower creation cap was measured, not chosen: a slice of 8 brand-new pages produced nothing on three attempts because the generator researches every page before writing and exhausted its budget mid-research, while a single new page was written in about six minutes.

At execution, consecutive same-kind slices of *different* areas are packed into one generator invocation of up to `MAX_PAGES_PER_INVOCATION` (8) pages, because every invocation pays a fixed planning pass (~$0.33 on Sonnet, 83% of a one-page run) and slices are per area; the slice remains the unit of the backlog and of carry-forward, two slices of the same area are never re-merged, and a one-area run is unchanged.

The governance gate's G13 (item #513, ADR-0003) enforces the disjoint scope of the bundle's two protection mechanisms: Claims certify generator-written facts on derived pages while `protected.yaml` fingerprints protect authoritative pages, so `claimsScopeFindings` in `scripts/openwiki-claims.mjs` fails an authoritative page carrying a Claims sidecar or a `.page-manifest.json` entry, a sidecar with no page, and a page carrying a front-matter `verified:` event with no sidecar.

The governance gate `scripts/check-openwiki-governance.mjs` runs rules G1–G13 (plus the fail-closed G0), not the G1–G12 range its original feature introduced: G13 (Claims scope) was added for item #513 under ADR-0003, so the documented rule range is G0–G13.
